s: Chapter three: Claude Code Configuration and Workflows
Before any theory, let's start with a story.
A contractor joins a team on a Monday.
She clones the repository.
She starts Claude Code.
And she asks it to add a new error type to the refund tool.
Claude writes something clean.
Sensible.
And completely wrong for this team.
It invents its own error categories.
It ignores the naming pattern everyone else uses.
The lead engineer is baffled.
On his laptop, Claude has followed those conventions perfectly for three weeks.
So he checks her setup.
Then his own.
And there it is.
Every one of those conventions lives in a file in his home folder.
It was never committed.
It never left his machine.
For three weeks, the team's standards had a membership of one.
That story is the whole of this chapter in miniature.
Claude Code behaves the way its files tell it to behave.
And one question keeps coming back.
Which file holds which instruction?
Who receives that file?
And when does it get read?
Get the location wrong, and the instruction silently goes missing for someone.
Get the loading wrong, and you pay for instructions nobody needed.
Or you miss the one that mattered.
This is Domain three of the Claude Certified Architect, Foundations exam.
Claude Code configuration and workflows.
It carries twenty percent of the exam.
So roughly one question in five.
We'll take it in six parts, one per official task statement.
Part one is the instruction file called CLAUDE.md, and how its levels stack.
Part two is custom slash commands and skills.
Part three is path-specific rules that load only for certain files.
Part four is when to plan first, and when to just do the work.
Part five is iterative refinement.
Meaning, how to make a loop of attempts actually converge.
Part six is running Claude Code inside automated pipelines.
Then a rapid trap round.
And a recap of ten things to remember.
One idea runs underneath all six parts.
So let me say it now.
Everything in this domain that is written as prose is advice.
Claude reads it.
Weighs it.
And usually follows it.
But none of it can stop anything from happening.
So when a question says something must happen every time, the answer is never a better-worded sentence.
It's code that runs at a fixed moment, and can say no.
Or, in four words.
Prose advises.
Code enforces.
Hold on to that.
It decides a surprising number of questions.
